summary: IMAP normally makes a client wait for a server continuation request before sending literal string data. This standards-track RFC specifies an alternate non-synchronizing literal form that avoids that network round trip, defining two IMAP extensions.

plainLanguage.summary:
IMAP has a way of sending a string whose length the client does not want to hard-code. The client sends the length, waits for the server to say it is ready, then sends the string. This RFC adds a marker to the length that says: do not wait, the data follows immediately.

Two versions are defined. One allows the short form anywhere. The other allows it only for small strings, which keeps a server from having to hold a very large amount of data in memory at once.

questions: what is the difference between literal+ and literal-
subtitle: Lets IMAP clients send string data without waiting for the server's go-ahead, saving a network round trip.

tldr.problem: In IMAP, when a client sends a string as a literal, it has to send the byte count, wait for the server to reply that it is ready, and only then send the data. On a slow or high-latency link that wait is paid again for every literal in the command.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a plus sign between the byte count and the closing brace. The server then reads the following bytes as part of the same command, with no continuation request and no waiting. Two capabilities are defined: LITERAL+, which allows this in all commands, and LITERAL-, which allows it only for literals of 4096 bytes or less.
tldr.outcome: A client can send a whole command in one go. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2088, which had defined only the LITERAL+ extension and had never been published as a Standards Track document.

today: RFC 7888 is a Proposed Standard from May 2016. It obsoletes RFC 2088 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The LITERAL+ and LITERAL- capabilities are registered in the IANA IMAP capabilities registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet Message Access Protocol contains the "literal" syntactic construct for communicating strings. When sending a literal from client to server, IMAP requires the client to wait for the server to send a command continuation request between sending the octet count and the string data. This document specifies an alternate form of literal that does not require this network round trip.

The document specifies two IMAP extensions. LITERAL+ allows the alternate form of literals, called non-synchronizing literals, in all IMAP commands. LITERAL- is the same as LITERAL+, but it disallows the alternate form of literals unless they are 4096 bytes or less.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is one character. Everything else about how the command is read stays the same.

sections.title: The Non-Synchronizing Literal Form
sections.content:
The non-synchronizing literal is added as an alternate form of literal, and it may appear in communication from client to server instead of the IMAP form, which is referred to as a synchronizing literal. The non-synchronizing literal form must not be sent from server to client.

Non-synchronizing literals may be used with any IMAP server implementation that returns "LITERAL+" or "LITERAL-" as one of the supported capabilities to the CAPABILITY command. If the server does not advertise either of those capabilities, the client can only use synchronizing literals.

The non-synchronizing literal is distinguished from the original synchronizing literal by having a plus sign between the octet count and the closing brace. The server does not generate a command continuation request in response to a non-synchronizing literal, and clients are not required to wait before sending the octets of one.

The protocol receiver of an IMAP server must check the end of every received line for an open brace followed by an octet count, a plus sign, and a close brace immediately preceding the CRLF. This sequence, if found, is the octet count of a non-synchronizing literal, and the server must treat the specified number of following octets and the following line as part of the same command.

It is important to note that the literal is not delimited by CRLF. It ends after the number of bytes specified by the octet count, and the current command continues from there. There might be a CRLF immediately after, which ends the command, or there might be more octets specifying other command parameters before the CRLF. If a space character is needed between parameters, it is important that the space appear after the literal, in its appropriate place.

A server may still process commands and reject errors on a line-by-line basis, as long as it checks for non-synchronizing literals at the end of each line. The formal syntax is literal = "{" number ["+"] "}" CRLF *CHAR8.
sections.plainLanguage: The server still reads the command a line at a time. What changes is that when a line ends with a byte count followed by a plus sign and a closing brace, the bytes after that line belong to the same command, so the server does not stop to send a go-ahead.

sections.title: When to Use and Not to Use Synchronizing Literals
sections.content:
Non-synchronizing literals have clear advantages for clients, such as simplicity of use, but they might be more difficult to handle on the server side. When a client uses a non-synchronizing literal that is too big for the server to accept, a server implementation that is compliant with LITERAL+ has to make a choice between a couple of non-optimal choices.

One choice is to read the number of bytes specified in the non-synchronizing literal and reject the command anyway; the server is allowed to send the tagged BAD or NO response before reading the whole literal, but this is quite wasteful of bandwidth if the literal is large. The other choice is to send an untagged BYE response explaining the reason for rejecting the literal, possibly accompanied by an ALERT response code, and close the connection. That forces the client to reconnect or report the error to the user, and in the latter case the error is unlikely to be understandable to the user. Some naive clients are known to blindly reconnect in this case and repeat the operation that caused the problem, introducing an infinite loop.

The problem is most common with the APPEND command, because most commands do not need to send lots of data from the client to the server. Some server implementations impose limits on literals, both synchronizing and non-synchronizing, accepted from clients in order to defend against denial-of-service attacks, and can generally impose much lower limits on literal sizes for all commands other than APPEND.

The situation can also be improved by implementing support for the APPENDLIMIT extension, which allows a server to advertise its APPEND limit, so that well-behaved clients can check it and avoid uploading big messages in the first place.
sections.plainLanguage: The trade-off is on the server. A client that sends a huge literal without waiting has already sent the data, so the server can only refuse it and throw the bytes away. Servers that worry about that advertise the LITERAL- capability instead.

sections.title: The LITERAL- Capability
sections.content:
The LITERAL- extension is almost identical to LITERAL+, with one exception: when LITERAL- is advertised, non-synchronizing literals used in any command must not be larger than 4096 bytes. Any literal larger than 4096 bytes must be sent as a synchronizing literal as specified in RFC 3501.

A server that is compliant with LITERAL- and encounters a non-synchronizing literal larger than 4096 bytes proceeds as described in the previous section. If responding to an APPEND command, the tagged BAD response must contain the TOOBIG response code. If responding with an untagged BYE response, it should include the TOOBIG response code. The form of the non-synchronizing literal does not change: it still uses the plus sign in the literal itself, even if the applicable extension is LITERAL-.

Because LITERAL- is a more restricted version of LITERAL+, IMAP servers must not advertise both of these capabilities at the same time. A server implementation can choose to have a configuration option to indicate which one to advertise.
sections.plainLanguage: LITERAL- is LITERAL+ with a ceiling. Strings up to 4096 bytes may still use the short form; anything bigger has to go the old way, so the server gets to decide how much data it will accept before the client starts sending.

sections.title: Interaction with Other IMAP Extensions
sections.content:
RFC 4466 updated the non-terminal "literal8" defined in RFC 3516 to allow non-synchronizing literals if both the BINARY extension and the LITERAL+ extension are supported by the server. This document also allows use of this extended "literal8" syntax when both the BINARY extension and the LITERAL- extension are supported by the server.

RFC 3502 describes the MULTIAPPEND extension and how it can be used with LITERAL+. The LITERAL- extension can be used with the MULTIAPPEND extension in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Two other extensions touch literals. The binary extension has its own literal form that can now also skip the wait, and the extension for appending several messages at once works with either of these capabilities.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Use of non-synchronizing literals can consume extra resources, such as memory, on IMAP servers and can be used for denial-of-service attacks. The LITERAL- extension partially improves this situation.

The document does not raise any security concerns beyond those raised by RFC 3501.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk is that a client can make the server hold a large amount of data without the server having agreed to it first. The size limit in LITERAL- is the mitigation.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IMAP4 capabilities are registered by publishing a Standards Track or IESG-approved Experimental RFC, and the registry is the IMAP capabilities registry at IANA.

IANA has updated the registry so that the reference for "LITERAL+" points to this document, and has added the "LITERAL-" capability with this document as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: Both capability names are registered with IANA so that a client can ask a server what it supports with the CAPABILITY command.

messages.label: LOGIN {11}
messages.note: The client sends the command with the byte count of the literal.

messages.label: Continuation request
messages.note: The server sends a command continuation request and the client waits for it.

messages.label: FRED FOOBAR {7}
messages.note: The client sends the second literal's byte count and waits again.

messages.label: Continuation request
messages.note: Another continuation request before the data may be sent.

messages.label: fat man
messages.note: The client finally sends the string data.

viz.caption: The same login with non-synchronizing literals, from the RFC's example

messages.label: LOGIN {11+} FRED FOOBAR {7+} fat man
messages.note: The plus sign after each byte count tells the server the data follows immediately, so the whole command goes out in one go.

messages.label: A001 OK LOGIN completed
messages.note: The server confirms the command, with no continuation request in between.

data.title: The literal production

           ; Number represents the number of CHAR8 octets
